title: Reia — The Road Back to Her Human
subtitle: A true USG story
summary: A personal account of Reia, separation, disappearance, a long search and the bond that survived distance, fear and hunger.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Personal account of Stefano De Tanini, preserved in correspondence with Dr. Flavio Bruno.

sections.heading: A beginning together
paragraphs: I brought Reia home when she was only twenty-five days old. She was tiny, dependent and completely new to the world around her. I cared for her, watched her grow and, for a long time, she lived beside me as naturally as if that had always been her place.

When Reia became an adult, however, a serious conflict developed with Hera, my first female and the dominant presence among my Cane Corso. Hera was deeply connected to me, but between the two females the tension became increasingly dangerous. Their confrontations were no longer ordinary disagreements. Neither was willing to surrender, and I understood that sooner or later one of them could be badly injured or killed.

sections.heading: The decision
paragraphs: My Cane Corso have their own shelters, but I do not want them to live chained or permanently confined. I could not ignore what was happening, and I had to make a decision. I could not part with Hera, so, believing I was protecting Reia, I gave her to a man who had earned my trust. He lived approximately 450 kilometres from the place where Reia had grown up.

It was one of the hardest decisions I had made. During her first week there, the man left Reia with his sheep. She escaped and disappeared into the forest. I cannot claim to know exactly what was in her mind, but I have always believed that she was trying to find her way back to me.

sections.heading: The first search
paragraphs: For three weeks there was nothing. Then someone photographed a Cane Corso in another town, about fifty kilometres from the place where Reia had been living, and posted the image online. It was Reia. I contacted the people who had seen her, asked where she had appeared and drove almost five hundred kilometres to search for her.

People from the area helped me. For almost twenty-four hours we searched. Finally I saw her, but the Reia standing in front of me was terrified. She did not respond normally even to my voice. She still recognised the sound of my car and would approach it, but every time I opened the door, fear became stronger than recognition and she ran again. I had to return home without her.

sections.heading: The second call
paragraphs: Two weeks later another photograph appeared. Reia had been seen again, this time in another town, roughly forty kilometres from the place of the first search. I contacted the man who had seen her. At seven in the evening I got into my car and left. I arrived at two in the morning.
This time she had been caught. After almost five weeks alone she no longer had the strength to run. She was painfully thin, exhausted and completely worn down.

sections.heading: She had not forgotten
paragraphs: When Reia saw me, she began making sounds I had never heard from her before, almost as if she were trying to speak. She wanted only to reach me and remain close to me. In that moment the distance, the weeks of searching and the exhaustion meant nothing. Reia had not forgotten.

I brought her home. Because she had spent weeks moving through forests, she was covered with ticks, so I kept her safely separated for a period while she was treated and recovered. A month later Reia was Reia again: strong, robust and full of life.

sections.heading: What Reia taught me
paragraphs: The experience changed me. Distance had not erased the bond. Fear had not erased it. Hunger had not erased it. Weeks alone had not erased it. Reia knew who her human was.

That is one of the reasons I cannot think of the Cane Corso as simply another dog. For me, Cane Corso means presence, loyalty, memory and a bond that becomes part of your life — and sometimes part of your heart.

title: The Dreams of a Boy
subtitle: Dr. Flavio Bruno — Memory & Heritage
summary: Dr. Flavio Bruno remembers the livestock fairs, rural families, working Cane Corso and an elderly veterinarian who shaped his life.
author: Dr. Flavio Bruno
source_credit: English adaptation of “I sogni di un ragazzo”, shared directly by Dr. Flavio Bruno.

sections.heading: A world of fairs and working animals
paragraphs: There was a time when livestock fairs were still part of everyday life in Southern Italy. They were places filled with voices, animals and practical knowledge. Landowners, butchers, livestock traders, farmers, veterinarians and curious visitors gathered among cattle, horses, pigs and poultry. And among them was the oldest companion of man: the dog.

One could see the Volpino, the Mastino Abruzzese and other working dogs of the South. But the animal that captured the imagination of the young Flavio Bruno more than any other was the powerful Cane Corso.

sections.heading: Diana and the old veterinarian
paragraphs: The uncle of Dr. Bruno's father spoke enthusiastically about his Cane Corso female, Diana. He remembered her strength, her form and especially her extraordinary grip, capable of stopping young cattle when they ran wildly through the farm.

As a boy, Bruno often accompanied an elderly village veterinarian. To him the man seemed almost like a magician: someone who could look at an animal, touch it and understand what others could not see. The veterinarian also knew how to speak with very different people, bringing knowledge and good humour wherever they went.

sections.heading: Learning through real dogs
paragraphs: References to the Cane Corso were frequent. Bruno saw many dogs and heard stories about Cane Corso belonging to families including Pettulli, De Matteis, Ianiri and Pappone. Conversations concerned temperament, incorruptible loyalty, psychological balance and functional versatility. Physical form was understood in relation to those qualities rather than apart from them.

The most valuable lessons came from watching the dogs in action. Under the guidance of the old veterinarian, the boy began to understand what he was seeing: not a static outline, but a body and character working together.

sections.heading: Families and colours
paragraphs: The fundamental physical and working qualities were recognisable, yet coat colours could differ from one family or farm to another. Bruno remembers fawn, ash-grey and black, as well as unusual brindles, combinations of grey, black and brown, darker coffee-like shades and very pale formentino. White markings could appear on the chest and feet.
These differences were part of a living rural population rather than a catalogue created for fashion. The dog still had to be useful.

sections.heading: The dream becomes a profession
paragraphs: The boy dreamed of becoming like his elderly veterinarian friend, remaining close to the practical and ancient world of the countryside, caring for animals and helping others appreciate the Cane Corso. Years later he enrolled in veterinary medicine. By then the old veterinarian had died, but the conversations remained with him.

Bruno continued walking through farms and countryside, observing dogs and people. He helped move dogs between farms and organised matings among Cane Corso, Mastini Abruzzesi and Volpini. He gave advice and received advice. The world he had dreamed of became his own life.

sections.heading: North and South
paragraphs: He later met enthusiasts from Central and Northern Italy, taking them to see dogs kept by shepherds, farmers and landowners. Two Cane Corso females — one from San Paolo di Civitate and one from Santa Croce di Magliano — were taken north under an agreement that puppies would later be returned to their original environment. The promised puppies never came back.

Bruno continued nevertheless, meeting enthusiasts across Molise, Abruzzo, Campania, Puglia, Sicily, Basilicata, Calabria and Sardinia. Cane Corso remained central, but conversations also included other Southern Italian working breeds and types.

sections.heading: The meaning of the dream
paragraphs: For many years Bruno believed that one day he would do something for the Cane Corso. With time he understood something else: the Cane Corso had also done something for him. It brought experience, people, places and knowledge into his life.
He became a veterinarian, like the man he had admired as a boy, and helped renew interest in the working dogs of his homeland. The dream had not disappeared. It had simply become his life.

title: Function Creates Type
subtitle: Understanding the Cane Corso through work, character and purpose
summary: The central Cane Corso Heritage principle: type becomes meaningful when body, temperament and function are read together.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Developed from the principle “La funzione fa il tipo” as explained by Dr. Flavio Bruno in correspondence with Stefano De Tanini.

sections.heading: A different first question
paragraphs: A Cane Corso cannot be understood by looking only at its outline. A photograph can show proportions. A measurement can tell us height. A pedigree can document ancestry. A standard can describe an ideal. But none of these, taken alone, can fully explain why the Cane Corso became what it is.
To understand type, we must first ask: what was the dog expected to do? This is the idea at the centre of Dr. Flavio Bruno's principle: “La funzione fa il tipo” — Function creates type.

sections.heading: Balance rather than exaggeration
paragraphs: In Dr. Bruno's explanation, the dog that truly represents type possesses a harmonious structure that reflects the character, aptitude and temperament associated with its function. He distinguishes this from hypertypical dogs, where traits become exaggerated, and hypotypical dogs, where important qualities of the type are missing.

The important word is balance: not size for the sake of size, not a dramatic head created only for appearance, not muscle without movement. The body must serve the dog and the dog must be capable of serving its purpose.

sections.heading: Form follows work
paragraphs: Working animals were historically selected because they could perform. Environment demanded certain qualities; work demanded others. Humans retained animals that were useful, reliable and capable. Over generations those choices influenced the body.

A dog expected to move, react and intervene required a different construction from a dog whose principal task was to remain with a flock and deter predators. Different work produced different behaviour, and different behaviour required different physical qualities.

sections.heading: Type is more than anatomy
paragraphs: If function creates type, then type cannot stop at the surface of the body. Temperament belongs to type. The ability to understand the situation belongs to type. The relationship with the human belongs to type. Courage must coexist with control; power with intelligence; construction with movement.

More weight does not automatically mean more Cane Corso. A more extreme head does not automatically mean more Cane Corso. Greater aggression does not automatically mean more Cane Corso. The animal must remain coherent.

sections.heading: Variation inside a functional population
paragraphs: Two Cane Corso do not need to look as if they were manufactured from the same mould. One may be somewhat taller; another more compact. Different families may repeatedly produce different expressions. Variation alone does not destroy type if the functional and behavioural qualities remain recognisable.

This principle also affects the study of local populations. Before declaring a local type, we must investigate history, territory, work and continuity. Function gives us a method for asking the question responsibly.

sections.heading: A living heritage
paragraphs: For Cane Corso Heritage, “Function Creates Type” is more than a slogan. It is a way of looking. Instead of asking only whether an animal matches an image, we ask why the body is built that way, what work demanded those qualities and what relationship existed between dog and human.

The Cane Corso was not created to become a photograph. Its appearance was the consequence of a life. Its body carried a purpose. Its character carried a purpose. Behind both stands the same principle: function creates type.

title: Coscienza
subtitle: The Cane Corso That Understands Without Words
summary: A reflection on the old idea of “coscienza”: attention, intelligence and silent communication between Cane Corso and human.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: The concept of “coscienza” comes from Dr. Flavio Bruno; the personal interpretation is by Stefano De Tanini.

sections.heading: A quality that cannot be measured
paragraphs: Height, weight and proportions can be measured. Some of the most important qualities of a Cane Corso cannot. They are experienced in the eyes, in attention and in the silence between the Cane Corso and the human beside it.

Dr. Flavio Bruno used a word that remained with me: “coscienza”. He explained that people once said a Cane Corso should possess this awareness — an intelligence so developed that it could understand its human without constant words. Sometimes a look was enough.

sections.heading: More than obedience
paragraphs: Obedience can be taught as a sequence: a word produces an action. Coscienza goes deeper. It is the capacity to observe, recognise intention, read movement and remain connected to the person beside the dog.
A relationship built only on commands can remain mechanical. A relationship built through years of living together becomes something else.

sections.heading: The language of a look
paragraphs: I recognised Dr. Bruno's description because I had experienced it with my own Cane Corso. Sometimes I do not need to raise my voice or repeat myself. A small movement of the hand, a change in posture or a look can be enough.
I try to communicate calmly, with consistency and respect. The voice is only one part of communication. The body speaks. Routine speaks. Trust speaks. Years spent together create their own language.

sections.heading: Intelligence in context
paragraphs: Working intelligence is not simply the ability to learn tricks. A functional Cane Corso had to observe its environment, distinguish ordinary life from the unusual and remain aware of the human beside it. Strength without awareness would have been dangerous. Courage without judgement would have been unreliable.
Power becomes useful only when it can be controlled, and control becomes meaningful when it is built on understanding.

sections.heading: The human also carries responsibility
paragraphs: It is easy to romanticise the idea of a dog that understands everything. That would be a mistake. If we expect the Cane Corso to understand us, our own behaviour must also be understandable. We cannot establish one rule today and the opposite tomorrow.
The relationship works in both directions. The Cane Corso learns the human, and the human must learn the Cane Corso.

sections.heading: A silent conversation
paragraphs: Perhaps “coscienza” cannot be translated perfectly by a single English word. Conscience, awareness, understanding, perception and intelligence each capture part of it.
The simplest image may be the best: a person stands beside a Cane Corso. No shouting. No repeated command. The person looks at the dog. The dog looks back. And both understand.

title: Living With a Cane Corso
subtitle: Responsibility Before Ownership
summary: A Cane Corso should begin with responsibility, not desire: time, boundaries, family, long-term care and the willingness to remain present when life becomes difficult.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: USG philosophy based on Stefano De Tanini’s personal practice and correspondence.

sections.heading: The first question
paragraphs: A Cane Corso should never begin with the question “Do I want one?” For me the first question is: “Am I prepared to be responsible for one?” There is an important difference between wanting a Cane Corso and being ready to live with one.
Appearance is easy to admire. The responsibility comes afterwards and lasts for years.

sections.heading: Responsibility does not end at the gate
paragraphs: When one of my puppies goes to another family, my responsibility does not suddenly disappear. I still want to know how the Cane Corso is developing, how it is treated and what relationship is forming with the people around it.
For this reason I try to remain in contact with many of the people who receive puppies from me. Responsibility does not end at the moment of placement.

sections.heading: I need to know the person first
paragraphs: When someone asks me for a Cane Corso, I begin by trying to understand the person: why they want one, where it will live, how they think about animals and whether they understand the physical and emotional responsibility.
If I believe a person is not suitable, I will not give them a Cane Corso. I would rather refuse than place one in hands I do not trust. Money cannot change that decision.

sections.heading: Strength changes the equation
paragraphs: Every owner owes responsibility to every animal, but physical power makes mistakes more serious. This is not an argument against the breed. It is an argument for taking the breed seriously.
Strength requires control; control requires education; education requires consistency. The relationship is being created from the beginning.

sections.heading: Education is not domination
paragraphs: I do not want a Cane Corso without character. The objective is not to destroy individuality until the animal becomes mechanically obedient. The objective is understanding. Boundaries and rules must exist, but the human must also be predictable.
Respect is not the same as fear. A frightened animal may obey to escape consequences; an animal that understands its person can respond from a relationship developed over time.

sections.heading: A Cane Corso is not for everyone
paragraphs: Admiring the breed does not mean everyone should own one. Sometimes respect means deciding that this is not the right Cane Corso, or not the right time in life for a Cane Corso.
Once a Cane Corso becomes dependent on you, the decision is no longer only about what you want. It is about the life placed in your hands.

title: From Puppy to Adult Cane Corso
subtitle: Growth, Movement, Character & Care
summary: A puppy develops body, mind, character and trust at the same time; responsible care protects all four.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Combines Stefano De Tanini’s observations with veterinary-cultural material shared by Dr. Flavio Bruno.

sections.heading: Growth is not a race
paragraphs: A powerful adult Cane Corso begins as a developing body with growing bones, changing muscles and an unfinished mind. Puppies do not all develop at the same pace. The goal should not be to create the largest puppy as quickly as possible, but to allow the Cane Corso to develop into a healthy, balanced adult.

sections.heading: The first world is the mother
paragraphs: Before the human begins to shape the puppy's life, the mother has already begun. Dr. Flavio Bruno describes weaning as a delicate transition: as the first teeth appear, the mother naturally spends more time away while the puppies move gradually toward independent feeding.
The larger lesson is to observe natural behaviour before rushing to interpret or interrupt it.

sections.heading: Health comes before appearance
paragraphs: Growth, parasite prevention, hygiene and the health of the mother and puppies belong to the same picture. Historical experience can teach us much, but diagnosis, vaccination, medication and individual treatment belong with a veterinarian who can assess the animal.

sections.heading: Movement builds body and mind
paragraphs: Dr. Bruno places strong emphasis on outdoor movement, light and muscular activity in puppy development. I understand this not as a demand for forced exercise, but as a reminder that safe movement and exposure to the real world help the puppy build coordination, confidence and awareness.

sections.heading: Character grows too
paragraphs: Every interaction teaches something. The way the human reacts, the environment, the family and ordinary routines all influence the developing Cane Corso. Body and mind develop together.

sections.heading: Do not hurry adulthood
paragraphs: A puppy may become physically large long before it becomes behaviourally mature. A large body can deceive the eye. Education, character and trust deserve patience even when the dog already looks imposing.

sections.heading: Science, conscience and nature
paragraphs: Science helps us understand; conscience reminds us of our responsibility; nature reminds us that Cane Corso is a living being with rhythms and needs of its own. Function does not begin on the day the adult is asked to work. Its foundation begins at birth.

title: The Mastino and the Cane Corso
subtitle: Two Strong Dogs, Two Different Functions
summary: A functional comparison between the Mastino Abruzzese and Cane Corso: both powerful, but shaped by different responsibilities.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Based on functional distinctions explained by Dr. Flavio Bruno.

sections.heading: The world of the Mastino
paragraphs: The traditional Mastino belonged to the world of the flock, shepherd, mountain pasture, masseria and predator. Its responsibility centred on the animals it protected. It did not simply arrive when danger appeared; it lived with the flock.

sections.heading: The dog that waits
paragraphs: Dr. Bruno uses the expression “cane d’attesa” for the functional logic of the Mastino: a dog of waiting. Waiting does not mean weakness. The Mastino watches, warns, occupies the space around the flock and discourages predators. If attack becomes unavoidable, it intervenes.

sections.heading: The world of the Cane Corso
paragraphs: Dr. Bruno contrasts this with the Cane Corso as a “cane d’attacco”, a dog associated with active intervention. The historical phrase should not be confused with modern indiscriminate aggression. It describes a working tradition in which the dog could be required to move toward a problem at the direction or need of the human.

sections.heading: Waiting and acting
paragraphs: The Mastino can be imagined as saying: “I am here. Do not come closer.” The Cane Corso: “If action is required, I will go.” This is an interpretation of the functional distinction, not a literal historical quotation. Both require courage, but courage is expressed differently.

sections.heading: Preserve the difference
paragraphs: Loving Cane Corso does not mean turning every old Italian working-dog story into a Cane Corso story. “Il grido della rabbia” concerns Mastini. The flock, shepherd, tratturo, wolf and masseria in that story belong to their world.
The Mastino should remain the Mastino. The Cane Corso should remain the Cane Corso. Understanding the difference makes both histories stronger.

title: The World of the Masseria
subtitle: Where Function Came Before Appearance
summary: The masseria helps explain why old working dogs were shaped by necessity, not by image.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Developed from Dr. Flavio Bruno’s material on Southern Italian rural life.

sections.heading: Look at the world around the dog
paragraphs: To understand the Cane Corso, we must sometimes stop looking at the Cane Corso and look at the world around it: land, animals, buildings, people, work, danger and daily necessity. Working dogs do not develop in isolation.

sections.heading: A practical agricultural world
paragraphs: The masseria was more than a building. People lived there, animals were kept, land was worked, food was produced and property had to be protected. Different dogs existed for different reasons: one could warn, another protect a flock, another stay close to the human and intervene in demanding tasks.

sections.heading: The Cane Corso beside the human
paragraphs: In Dr. Bruno's descriptions, Cane Corso appears close to guardians, farmers, hunters, landowners and people whose daily work required a strong, intelligent and reliable animal. This helps explain why character matters as much as anatomy.

sections.heading: Usefulness shapes anatomy
paragraphs: Power mattered, but excessive mass could interfere with work. Strong jaws mattered, but the rest of the body had to carry them. Muscle mattered, but the dog still had to move. Courage mattered, but uncontrolled aggression could destroy usefulness.

sections.heading: Heritage includes the environment
paragraphs: Cane Corso Heritage should therefore preserve more than the animal. It should preserve the people, work, land and practical system that explain the animal. When that world disappears from memory, part of the explanation for Cane Corso disappears with it.

title: The Porcaio and the Cane Corso
subtitle: A Forgotten Working Partnership
summary: A forgotten Southern Italian occupation shows Cane Corso intelligence through long daily work with village pigs.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Based on “Il Meridione”, material shared by Dr. Flavio Bruno.

sections.heading: The porcaio
paragraphs: In some Southern Italian villages there was once a figure whose work is difficult to imagine today: the porcaio. Early in the morning he moved through the village collecting pigs belonging to different families. By day the animals became one large group, a “morra”.

sections.heading: A village herd
paragraphs: Dr. Flavio Bruno describes a porcaio capable of managing up to one hundred pigs with the help of one Cane Corso or at most a pair. The pigs were taken into woods and scrubland to graze, then guided home in the evening.

sections.heading: Intelligence revealed through work
paragraphs: Long days and months together created mutual understanding between human and Cane Corso. This is where intelligence becomes difficult to fake. A dog that constantly requires correction is inefficient; a dog that cannot read movement and direction becomes a burden.

sections.heading: Protection as part of the job
paragraphs: The Cane Corso also protected pigs from dangers that could include predators, roaming dogs, thieves and, in the account, encounters with wild boar. The dog therefore needed endurance, courage and judgement.

sections.heading: A complete rural economy
paragraphs: Payment to the porcaio could be made in grain or maize. Grain became flour and bran; bread was made for the household and a rougher “pane canino” could also be prepared for dogs. The Cane Corso was woven into the same economy as the people and livestock around it.

sections.heading: Work creates understanding
paragraphs: There were no trophies and no audience. The reward was that the work was completed. The porcaio and his Cane Corso remind us that some qualities of a working breed become visible only when there is something real to do.

title: The Horse, the Guardian and the Cane Corso
subtitle: Protection in the Great Rural Estates
summary: On large estates, the horse provided movement while Cane Corso protected people, property and valuable animals.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Based on Dr. Flavio Bruno’s account of Cane Corso among Southern Italian landowners, horse herds and guardians.

sections.heading: Two valuable animals
paragraphs: In the rural world described by Dr. Flavio Bruno, major landowners valued two animals in particular: the horse and the Cane Corso. The horse provided movement, transport, work and hunting. The Cane Corso provided security.

sections.heading: Protection of wealth
paragraphs: Horses were valuable and therefore attractive to thieves. Where horses lived across large properties, human supervision could not be everywhere at once. A courageous dog capable of remaining alert by day and night had real economic importance.

sections.heading: Finding and holding livestock
paragraphs: Dr. Bruno also describes Cane Corso used to locate animals lost in dense vegetation or woodland and hold them until a guardian arrived, using a controlled grip rather than killing the animal. The historical value lies in the relationship between physical power and purpose.

sections.heading: The meaning of control
paragraphs: Power without control is incomplete. The useful working animal was valuable because strength could be applied to a task and remain connected to the human who directed it.

title: Colour Is Not Type
subtitle: Look at the Whole Cane Corso
summary: Coat colour belongs to heritage, but it cannot replace health, character, movement, structure or function.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Developed from Dr. Flavio Bruno’s guidance and Stefano De Tanini’s personal observations.

sections.heading: The attraction of colour
paragraphs: Colour catches the eye immediately: black, grey, fawn, formentino, brindle. Sometimes people begin searching for the colour before they begin searching for the Cane Corso. For me, that reverses the correct order.

sections.heading: Look at the whole animal
paragraphs: Dr. Flavio Bruno advised that the choice of a puppy should not be dominated by colour, but should consider the animal as a whole. Type, proportions, character, aptitude and temperament belong together.

sections.heading: Colour can still tell history
paragraphs: Dr. Bruno's memories include black, fawn, ash-grey and several forms of brindling, with colour tendencies sometimes differing among families or farms. This makes colour historically interesting without making it primary.

sections.heading: My own observations
paragraphs: I became curious about inheritance through my own Cane Corso and different pairings, but I have always treated those observations as personal experience rather than scientific conclusions. Health, character, structure, function and what an animal transmits over time remain more important.

sections.heading: Choose the Cane Corso, not the paint
paragraphs: A beautiful colour cannot compensate for poor health, unstable character or a body that cannot move properly. Heritage can preserve colour memories without allowing fashion to turn one coat into a substitute for type.

title: Choosing a Cane Corso
subtitle: Look Beyond the First Impression
summary: Choose years of shared life, not a photograph: look at the whole animal, the family and the human responsibility.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: USG editorial philosophy based on Stefano De Tanini’s experience and Dr. Flavio Bruno’s emphasis on the whole animal.

sections.heading: Do not begin with the photograph
paragraphs: Choosing a Cane Corso should not begin with colour, size or the most dramatic image. A Cane Corso will live beside you long after the first photograph has been forgotten.

sections.heading: Look at the family
paragraphs: I want to understand what stands behind the individual: parents, previous generations when known, character, health, structure, behaviour and consistency of traits. A single beautiful animal tells less than a family observed over time.

sections.heading: Character matters from the beginning
paragraphs: The largest puppy is not automatically the best choice. I would rather watch how a puppy responds, recovers from unfamiliar situations, interacts and observes. A puppy is still developing, so there is no magic test, but the questions matter.

sections.heading: Choose the human too
paragraphs: When I place a Cane Corso with another person, I also evaluate the person. Why do they want one? Do they understand the responsibility? If I do not trust the situation, I prefer not to place the puppy.

sections.heading: Years, not minutes
paragraphs: You are not choosing an image. You are choosing years of shared life. That decision deserves more patience than excitement alone.

title: The First Days Together
subtitle: Begin With Observation, Consistency and Trust
summary: The first days are not about proving strength. They are about establishing clear expectations and beginning a relationship.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Editorial synthesis of Stefano De Tanini’s stated philosophy; not a day-by-day training protocol.

sections.heading: Begin with relationship
paragraphs: The first days with a Cane Corso should not be about proving who is stronger. Everything is new: place, people, sounds, routine and expectations. The Cane Corso is already studying all of them.

sections.heading: Do not create rules you will later destroy
paragraphs: If something will not be acceptable when the Cane Corso is a powerful adult, think carefully before encouraging it as a puppy. The puppy does not understand that humans sometimes change rules only because its body has become larger.

sections.heading: Observe before demanding
paragraphs: The first days are a chance for the human to learn the individual. What creates confidence? What causes uncertainty? How does the puppy communicate? There is already a character developing.

sections.heading: Presence matters
paragraphs: Living together creates the language that later seems almost silent. The Cane Corso watches the human; the human learns the Cane Corso. Over time, gestures, looks and routines begin to carry meaning.

sections.heading: Trust before perfection
paragraphs: The first days do not need to produce a finished Cane Corso. They need to establish a direction: clear boundaries, calm communication, safety, observation and trust. The rest takes time.

title: Motherhood and Weaning
subtitle: Respecting a Natural Transition
summary: Weaning is a gradual biological and behavioural transition that deserves observation, hygiene and veterinary responsibility.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Based on material by Dr. Flavio Bruno concerning maternity, weaning, growth and prevention.

sections.heading: A litter teaches patience
paragraphs: Birth is dramatic and easy to remember, but the quieter weeks that follow are just as important. The mother feeds, cleans, protects, moves away, returns and gradually prepares her puppies for a life in which she will no longer provide everything.

sections.heading: A gradual transition
paragraphs: Dr. Flavio Bruno describes weaning as delicate rather than sudden. As the first teeth appear, the mother naturally begins to spend more time away while puppies move toward a new form of feeding.

sections.heading: Observe the mother
paragraphs: Humans often want to control everything, but the mother is communicating too. Her willingness to remain with the litter changes. Dr. Bruno also describes regurgitation of partially digested food as a natural canid behaviour that can appear during weaning.

sections.heading: Health surrounds the litter
paragraphs: The mother's health, environment, hygiene, parasite prevention and the condition of the puppies belong to the same picture. Experience should work together with veterinary medicine, not replace it.

sections.heading: More than food
paragraphs: The puppy is not only changing diet. It is becoming more independent and learning new relationships with littermates, humans and the environment. The transition should not become a race.

sections.heading: Science, conscience and nature
paragraphs: Nature gives us processes; science helps us understand them; conscience reminds us that the lives involved depend on our decisions.

title: The Cane Corso and the Family
subtitle: Presence, Relationship and Responsibility
summary: A Cane Corso becomes part of household rhythm, which makes family consistency and responsibility essential.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Based on Stefano De Tanini’s daily-life observations and USG philosophy.

sections.heading: Part of the household rhythm
paragraphs: For me, a Cane Corso does not live beside a family as a piece of property. It learns people, voices, movements, routines, doors opening, cars arriving and the atmosphere of ordinary days.

sections.heading: The family teaches every day
paragraphs: Training sessions are not the only education a Cane Corso receives. Ordinary life teaches constantly: who sets limits, who rewards, who changes the rules, who becomes nervous, who remains calm.

sections.heading: Consistency gives security
paragraphs: A Cane Corso should not receive completely contradictory expectations from different family members. Clear, humane consistency helps the animal understand the household.

sections.heading: Belonging creates responsibility
paragraphs: A close family bond is beautiful, but affection does not remove the need for boundaries. Trust does not eliminate responsibility. Physical strength does not become harmless simply because the Cane Corso is loving at home.

sections.heading: Relationship before image
paragraphs: This is why Cane Corso Heritage should show more than the dramatic guardian image. Daily presence, quiet companionship and understanding are also part of the breed's life beside humans.

title: Guardianship Without Uncontrolled Aggression
subtitle: Strength Is Valuable Only When It Has Direction
summary: Historical courage should be understood as purposeful character, not as a reason to manufacture aggression in a modern Cane Corso.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: USG interpretation of historical functional material shared by Dr. Flavio Bruno.

sections.heading: The wrong attraction
paragraphs: Words such as powerful, protective and formidable can attract the wrong kind of admiration. Some people imagine that more aggression must mean a better guardian. I do not believe that.

sections.heading: Historical courage had a purpose
paragraphs: Dr. Flavio Bruno describes Cane Corso as a dog capable of direct intervention in historical work, contrasted with the Mastino Abruzzese whose flock-guarding role relied heavily on deterrence and holding position. Historical function should not be confused with modern indiscriminate attack behaviour.

sections.heading: Confidence is different from instability
paragraphs: A stable guardian should be capable of existing peacefully when there is no threat. Calmness is part of control. Observation is part of intelligence. Connection with the human is part of the working relationship.

sections.heading: Do not manufacture aggression
paragraphs: A Cane Corso already possesses physical power. We do not need to create conflict to prove it. The responsibility of the human is to create stability, rules, experience, control and trust.

sections.heading: The strongest response may be restraint
paragraphs: Sometimes courage is action. Sometimes the correct behaviour is to stand still and do nothing. The value lies in responding appropriately. For USG, guardianship means controlled strength, not theatre or intimidation.

title: The Rustic Cane Corso
subtitle: Function Before Perfection
summary: Rustic should mean practical, resilient and functional — not undocumented quality by default and never neglected health.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Developed from Dr. Flavio Bruno’s distinction between rustic/functional and modern selection.

sections.heading: What rustic does not mean
paragraphs: One of the first distinctions Dr. Flavio Bruno asked me to consider was between rustic, functional dogs and dogs selected primarily in modern institutional environments. But rustic does not mean neglected, unhealthy or automatically valuable because documentation is missing.

sections.heading: Variation is not automatically failure
paragraphs: A functional population may contain variation. Some animals may be taller, some more compact, some heavier and some more athletic. Dr. Bruno argues that anatomical variation can coexist with recognisable functional and character qualities.

sections.heading: Study before declaring
paragraphs: When I asked whether a Bulgarian local type might exist, Dr. Bruno pointed to questions that must come first: how long the dogs have been present, where they came from, who used them, what work they performed and whether continuity can be documented.

sections.heading: Rustic should still mean healthy
paragraphs: Function cannot survive without health. A chronically unsound animal is not made more authentic by calling it rustic. The body must work and the animal must be capable of living the life expected of it.

sections.heading: An unfinished question
paragraphs: The Bulgarian dogs I have observed deserve study, but study should remain study until evidence tells us more. Heritage should create better questions before it creates confident conclusions.

title: Before the Standard, the Cane Corso Was Already There
subtitle: Mario Monti, Drago and Milan 1914
summary: A documentary draft on the reported 1914 Milan episode and the difference between historical existence and later official recognition.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Based on historical material shared by Dr. Flavio Bruno; independent source verification is still required.

sections.heading: The question
paragraphs: Does a breed begin to exist when an institution recognises it, or does recognition arrive because something already exists? Historical material shared by Dr. Flavio Bruno makes that question impossible to ignore.

sections.heading: Milan 1914
paragraphs: According to the material provided by Dr. Bruno, Mario Monti of Bagnacavallo entered a dog named Drago as a Cane Corso at a Milan exhibition in 1914. The judge reportedly refused to evaluate the animal because the kennel institution had no recognised standard for the breed.

sections.heading: Monti points to reality
paragraphs: The response attributed to Monti points away from the institution and toward lived reality: travel through Italy, move south, observe dogs used by guards and private citizens, and the Cane Corso would be found in increasing numbers, particularly around Naples and other Southern areas.

sections.heading: Recognition and origin are not the same thing
paragraphs: Official recognition can provide a common reference and documentation, but it cannot create a historical working population retroactively. If the Cane Corso existed as a working type before standardisation, later recognition belongs to another stage of the story.

sections.heading: People before institutions
paragraphs: Before formal recognition, practical users selected animals according to usefulness, character and function. Documentation may have been imperfect or absent, but the mechanism of human selection was real.

sections.heading: Verification remains essential
paragraphs: This article remains a documentary draft. Period publication details, names, dates and wording connected with the episode must be independently verified before the material is presented as definitive historical bibliography.

title: The Cane Corso in Words and Images
subtitle: When a Breed Enters Cultural Memory
summary: Literature, dictionaries, paintings and other cultural traces can support heritage research when provenance and context are treated honestly.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Based on documentary material and research principles discussed with Dr. Flavio Bruno.

sections.heading: A breed leaves cultural traces
paragraphs: A working animal leaves more than descendants. It leaves words, stories, paintings, descriptions, proverbs, comparisons and fragments inside books. These traces can survive long after the working world that produced them has changed.

sections.heading: Language remembers reputation
paragraphs: Dr. Flavio Bruno has shared references in which the Cane Corso name appears in older literature and vocabulary. Such references can be historically valuable because a breed name used as a comparison suggests that the audience understood the reputation attached to it.

sections.heading: Images require caution
paragraphs: Iconography is fascinating but dangerous when overinterpreted. A strong dog in an old painting may resemble Cane Corso, but resemblance alone does not establish identity. Attribution, date, context and provenance matter.

sections.heading: Unknown should remain unknown
paragraphs: Dr. Bruno once shared a painting he had bought in Naples years earlier but could no longer identify by author or date. The image can remain interesting without being presented as more precisely documented than it is.

sections.heading: A future documentary archive
paragraphs: Cane Corso Heritage should one day contain a structured archive: verified bibliographic references, vocabulary, period publications, historical photographs, artwork with known provenance and a separate area for uncertain or comparative evidence.

sections.heading: Passion and discipline
paragraphs: Without passion we would never search. Without discipline we might believe everything we find. USG should have both.

title: Il Grido della Rabbia
subtitle: The Cry of Rabies
summary: A tragic rural story of Leone, a Mastino who intercepted a wolf attack and saved a shepherd, at the cost of his own life.
author: Dr. Flavio Bruno
source_credit: English adaptation of the true story “Il grido della rabbia” shared by Dr. Flavio Bruno.

sections.heading: The world of the Mastini
paragraphs: An old shepherd told a story from the territory around Morrone del Sannio, a landscape of flocks, masserie, wolves and Mastini. These dogs were not decorative. They protected sheep and, sometimes, human lives.

sections.heading: Leone
paragraphs: Among the family's Mastini was Leone, the dominant male. He was remembered as active, deeply attached to his human and dependable in work. One day near the edge of the grazing land, the shepherd heard a strange, continuous cry from the direction of the woods.

sections.heading: The attack
paragraphs: A wolf came toward the shepherd. Leone reacted immediately, intercepting the attack. The wolf behaved abnormally: its eyes, saliva, isolation and willingness to attack a human created fear that something was wrong. Other Mastini joined the fight and the wolf was killed.

sections.heading: The wound
paragraphs: Leone had been bitten. The wound itself did not initially seem catastrophic, but the wolf's strange behaviour remained in the shepherd's mind. The incident was reported to the veterinarian.

sections.heading: The cry of rabies
paragraphs: According to the account preserved by Dr. Bruno, the veterinarian warned that the characteristic “cry of rabies” required suspicion of the disease. Leone, having been exposed, had to be isolated and observed under the rules of that period.

sections.heading: The loss
paragraphs: The shepherd waited through the longest days of his life. Symptoms eventually appeared and Leone was killed according to the rules then in force. The animal that had saved the shepherd could not be saved.

sections.heading: Sentinella
paragraphs: The following day the grieving shepherd sat beneath a large oak. Sentinella, Leone's female, approached and pressed herself against him. When she rolled onto her back, he realised she was pregnant. The family kept the entire litter; two puppies were remembered as almost identical to their father.

sections.heading: What remains
paragraphs: Leone was gone, but his blood, descendants and memory remained. This is a Mastino story, not a Cane Corso story, and keeping that distinction is part of respecting the memory entrusted to us.

title: Spezzaferro
subtitle: The Mastino Who Chose His Human
summary: The story of an old shepherd, a Mastino who broke a chain to return to him, and a final walk into the forest.
author: Dr. Flavio Bruno
source_credit: English adaptation of “Spezzaferro”, shared by Dr. Flavio Bruno.

sections.heading: Pasquale and his Mastino
paragraphs: Pasquale was a shepherd who travelled to work on different masserie, always taking his Mastino with him. The dog came from a large massaro of upper Molise whose family had practised transhumance for generations. Pasquale obtained him by barter, exchanging a young pig.

sections.heading: A life of work
paragraphs: The Mastino grew up on the foods of that rural world and became known for strength and intelligence. Pasquale and the dog worked together for years.

sections.heading: The painful decision
paragraphs: Age eventually prevented Pasquale from continuing with the sheep. Believing the Mastino would be better spending his final years at the farm, Pasquale left him there. To prevent the dog from following, he tied him with a chain.

sections.heading: The next morning
paragraphs: The following morning Pasquale found the Mastino outside his door in the village. The dog had broken the chain and returned to his human. Pasquale's son gave him the name that remained: Spezzaferro — Iron-breaker.

sections.heading: Two old lives
paragraphs: Man and Mastino grew old together. Then Pasquale died. Spezzaferro continued sleeping beneath the window of the man he had loved. After the funeral, as the bells sounded for the dead, the old Mastino waited with the people and accompanied the procession toward the cemetery.

sections.heading: The final walk
paragraphs: One late-autumn day Pasquale's son watched Spezzaferro walk slowly and calmly toward the nearby forest. He disappeared among the trees and never returned. In the story preserved by Dr. Bruno, he was twenty years old.

sections.heading: The heart of the story
paragraphs: The exact age belongs to the testimony and should remain there rather than being transformed into a scientific claim. The heart of the story is simpler: the Mastino could have remained at the farm, but he chose the old man he loved. The chain could hold his body for a night; it could not decide where he belonged.

title: Cane da Presa
subtitle: When the Name Describes the Function
summary: “Cane da presa” is treated here as functional terminology connected with gripping and holding, not as a separate modern breed label.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Based on terminology explained by Dr. Flavio Bruno in correspondence.

sections.heading: A confusing term
paragraphs: When I first began looking more deeply into Cane Corso history, the expression “cane da presa” created questions. Was it another breed, another type or another historical name?

sections.heading: Name and function
paragraphs: Through correspondence with Dr. Flavio Bruno, the distinction became clearer: Cane Corso is the name of the dog; “cane da presa” describes a function connected with a powerful grip and the ability to hold.

sections.heading: The grip had a purpose
paragraphs: Historical catch work should not be romanticised as uncontrolled biting. A useful dog held because a human task required restraint — in work with livestock, dangerous animals or hunting contexts. The grip was a tool.

sections.heading: The body behind the function
paragraphs: A powerful hold requires more than teeth. Head, jaws, neck, body, balance, confidence and willingness to remain engaged all work together. Function helps explain anatomy.

sections.heading: Historical understanding, modern responsibility
paragraphs: Studying the old function does not mean modern owners should manufacture biting situations. Historical function helps us understand the breed; modern responsibility determines how we live with it today.

title: What Makes a Cane Corso?
subtitle: A Question Larger Than a Standard
summary: Cane Corso identity is found in the relationship between type, function, character, temperament, structure, movement and the bond with humans.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: USG editorial synthesis based on correspondence with Dr. Flavio Bruno and Stefano De Tanini’s observations.

sections.heading: A larger question
paragraphs: The longer I study Cane Corso, the less interested I become in the question “Does this dog match a photograph?” I prefer a more difficult question: “What makes this a Cane Corso?”

sections.heading: No single feature is enough
paragraphs: Dr. Flavio Bruno's explanations repeatedly return to type, function, character, temperament, aptitude, structure and balance. For me, Cane Corso cannot be reduced to one head, one colour, one weight, one document or even one working behaviour.

sections.heading: Harmony
paragraphs: A correct animal should make sense as a whole. Extreme mass does not automatically create strength. Extreme aggression does not automatically create courage. A dramatic head attached to a body that cannot move properly does not create balance.

sections.heading: Character belongs to type
paragraphs: Character is easy to ignore in a photograph, but intelligence, awareness, courage, attachment and control belong to Cane Corso. Remove all of that and preserve only the outline, and something essential may have been lost.

sections.heading: A living definition
paragraphs: Perhaps Cane Corso cannot be understood through a single sentence. But I have reached one conclusion: a Cane Corso should make sense in motion, in character and beside its human, not only while standing for inspection.

title: The Cane Corso of Southern Italy
subtitle: A Dog Inside the Life of the Meridione
summary: The Cane Corso of the Meridione appears inside a network of villages, estates, livestock, hunting, guarding and ordinary human work.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Based on Dr. Flavio Bruno’s material concerning the working Cane Corso and the rural culture of Southern Italy.

sections.heading: Study the South
paragraphs: To understand the traditional Cane Corso, we cannot study only the animal. We must study the Meridione: villages, landowners, farmers, livestock, forests, hunters, guardians, poverty, wealth, dangers and the work that had to be done every day.

sections.heading: One dog, many forms of work
paragraphs: In Dr. Bruno's account the Cane Corso appears with pigs, around horses, beside guardians, on rural estates, in hunting and in protection. These roles demanded a common group of qualities: strength, courage, intelligence, endurance, determination and cooperation with humans.

sections.heading: Not one social class
paragraphs: The Cane Corso cannot be reduced to the dog of one class of people. Different practical users required different tasks, but usefulness remained central. A landowner might value protection of property and horses; a porcaio needed intelligence and stamina; a hunter required another expression of the same functional character.

sections.heading: The South was not uniform
paragraphs: Molise was not Campania, and Campania was not Puglia. Mountain communities differed from plains, coastal areas from inland territories. Local families had different preferences. Functional populations can therefore show variation without automatically becoming different breeds.

sections.heading: Ordinary life preserves heritage
paragraphs: The Cane Corso survived not only in books but in ordinary life: family memory, farms, stories and decisions about which animals were useful enough to continue. The history of Cane Corso is also the history of its relationship with the people of the South.

title: The Old Families and Their Colours
subtitle: Diversity Inside a Functional Type
summary: Memories of Pettulli, De Matteis, Ianiri and Pappone show a working population with recognisable qualities and varied coat traditions.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Developed from Dr. Flavio Bruno’s memories in “I sogni di un ragazzo”.

sections.heading: Families, not a visual template
paragraphs: When Dr. Flavio Bruno recalls the Cane Corso of his youth, he does not describe an identical population produced from one visual mould. He remembers families, farms, territories and individual dogs.

sections.heading: Names preserved in memory
paragraphs: Among the names he shared are Pettulli, De Matteis, Ianiri and Pappone. They form part of the human network through which Cane Corso were known, observed and exchanged.

sections.heading: Working qualities and colour variation
paragraphs: Dr. Bruno remembers recognisable physical and working qualities, while coat colour could vary significantly among families or farms: fawn, ash-grey, black, different brindles, grey-black-brown combinations, darker coffee-like shades and very pale formentino.

sections.heading: Colour should be remembered, not worshipped
paragraphs: There is an important difference between saying a colour was remembered in a historical working population and saying that colour makes a Cane Corso superior. The first is heritage; the second is fashion.

sections.heading: Preserve the family names honestly
paragraphs: The old family names deserve preservation even when genetic continuity cannot be reconstructed. We should never invent an unbroken line where documentation does not exist. Memory remains valuable when it is labelled as memory.

title: Functional Selection and Modern Selection
subtitle: Two Different Ways of Looking at a Cane Corso
summary: A neutral editorial framing of Dr. Flavio Bruno’s documented criticism of selection that prioritises exhibition or commerce over function.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Dr. Flavio Bruno’s criticisms are presented as his views; editorial framing by Stefano De Tanini.

sections.heading: Practical users
paragraphs: Dr. Flavio Bruno distinguishes historical practical users — landowners, hunters, guardians, butchers and others — from modern systems in which dogs may be evaluated primarily through exhibition, titles or commercial value. For practical users, usefulness was immediate and unavoidable.

sections.heading: Dr. Bruno’s criticism
paragraphs: Dr. Bruno is strongly critical of aspects of ENCI-oriented and show-oriented selection. He argues that excessive emphasis on exhibition, commercial value and exaggerated morphology can move selection away from a functional Cane Corso. Cane Corso Heritage presents these claims as his documented perspective, not as an institutional verdict.

sections.heading: A more useful question
paragraphs: Instead of reducing the discussion to “show versus working”, I prefer to ask: what qualities are we actually selecting? Health, movement, character, temperament, structure, functional ability and family continuity keep the whole animal visible.

sections.heading: Standards and pedigrees as tools
paragraphs: Standards can provide common language. Pedigrees can preserve ancestry. Documentation can be valuable. The problem begins when the document becomes more important than the living animal. For USG, these systems are tools, not substitutes for observation.

sections.heading: Balance
paragraphs: The concepts hypertypical, hypotypical and in type provide one way to discuss balance. The point is not to attack institutions or breeders, but to keep asking whether the Cane Corso remains healthy, coherent and functional.

sections.heading: No war is needed
paragraphs: USG should not exist to attack clubs, judges or breeders, nor to defend them automatically. The purpose is understanding: study the history, the function, the body and the character, and support conclusions with evidence wherever possible.

title: The Bulgarian Question
subtitle: Could a Local Cane Corso Type Exist?
summary: A research question, not a conclusion: could long-term function, territory and continuity have produced a local Cane Corso expression in Bulgaria?
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Open research question discussed with Dr. Flavio Bruno; not an established claim.

sections.heading: The observation
paragraphs: I have observed Cane Corso in different parts of Bulgaria that differ in height, mass, head, movement and character. Those differences made me ask whether a local Bulgarian type could exist — not a new breed and not an alternative standard, but a local functional direction.

sections.heading: The question is not the answer
paragraphs: Dr. Flavio Bruno did not offer an easy conclusion. He asked what would need to be investigated: when the dogs arrived, where they came from, whether later Italian dogs were introduced, who kept them, what work they performed and whether continuity can be demonstrated.

sections.heading: A type needs history
paragraphs: A few similar-looking animals do not create a local type. Neither does a large male or a group of undocumented dogs. Serious study would require time depth, geography, family relationships, testimony, old photographs and possibly genetic evidence if such a project became realistic.

sections.heading: Function would matter
paragraphs: If Cane Corso remained in a territory and continued performing particular work, function and environment could contribute to preserving a local expression. This is where “Function creates type” becomes a research method rather than a slogan.

sections.heading: No legend in advance
paragraphs: It would be easy to create a dramatic Bulgarian Cane Corso story and repeat it until people believe it. That is exactly what USG should not do. Evidence must lead the conclusion, not the other way around.

sections.heading: A future USG project
paragraphs: A future project could collect old photographs, known imports, family histories, dates, locations and descriptions of work. The goal would not be to prove a predetermined answer, but to discover what the evidence allows us to say.

title: Science, Conscience and Nature
subtitle: A Philosophy of Care
summary: Three ideas — evidence, responsibility and respect for the living animal — form a useful framework for Cane Corso care.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Inspired by Dr. Flavio Bruno’s veterinary-cultural material “Prevenzione e cura secondo scienza, coscienza e natura”.

sections.heading: Science
paragraphs: Science asks us to learn, observe evidence, understand development, recognise disease and use veterinary knowledge when an animal requires help. Tradition can preserve valuable experience, but experience should not prevent us from learning something new.

sections.heading: Conscience
paragraphs: Knowledge without responsibility is not enough. The Cane Corso depends on human decisions: which animals reproduce, how mothers are cared for, how puppies are raised, when veterinary assistance is sought and where puppies go.

sections.heading: Nature
paragraphs: The Cane Corso is not a machine. Growth has rhythms, motherhood has behaviour, puppies develop gradually and individuals mature at different rates. Human care should protect these processes rather than pretend everything can be forced to a timetable.

sections.heading: Function begins inside the body
paragraphs: A functional Cane Corso requires a body capable of living and moving well. Preserving a working breed does not mean demanding suffering in the name of tradition; it means protecting physical solidity, movement, reproductive health and stable temperament.

sections.heading: Prevention is daily
paragraphs: Prevention begins with attention: what is normal for this Cane Corso, how is it growing, how is it moving, how is the mother recovering, how are the puppies developing? Observation cannot replace veterinary medicine, but it can make us better guardians of wellbeing.

sections.heading: The three belong together
paragraphs: Science without conscience can become cold. Conscience without knowledge can make good intentions dangerous. Nature without responsibility can become an excuse for neglect. Together they create balance.

title: Movement, Air and Growth
subtitle: Raising a Body That Can Function
summary: Movement and outdoor experience should support healthy development, coordination and confidence without turning puppy growth into a race.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Developed from Dr. Flavio Bruno’s material on movement, light, hygiene and puppy growth.

sections.heading: A living body
paragraphs: A Cane Corso puppy is not a statue under construction. It is a living body learning how to use itself. Dr. Flavio Bruno places importance on outdoor movement, muscular activity, natural light and general hygiene in robust development.

sections.heading: More is not automatically better
paragraphs: A developing puppy does not need to become an athlete as quickly as possible. Growth needs movement, but also time. The purpose is natural exploration, coordination and confidence, not exhaustion.

sections.heading: Movement develops the mind
paragraphs: Outdoor life offers sounds, smells, surfaces, weather, distance, people and unexpected situations. The puppy is building mental experience at the same time as physical coordination.

sections.heading: Watch the individual
paragraphs: One Cane Corso may tire sooner than another. Growth phases differ. Pain, persistent lameness or significant difficulty should not be treated as something the puppy must simply work through. Function depends on health.

sections.heading: Build for a lifetime
paragraphs: The goal is not the strongest six-month-old puppy. The goal is an adult whose body can serve it for years. Movement should support coordination, confidence, muscular development and mobility.

title: Feeding the Cane Corso
subtitle: Tradition, Quality and Modern Responsibility
summary: Historical feeding traditions can teach context, while modern feeding decisions must consider safety, balance and the individual Cane Corso.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: Historical material by Dr. Flavio Bruno plus Stefano De Tanini’s personal feeding philosophy.

sections.heading: Beyond feeding camps
paragraphs: Food is one of the easiest subjects on which people become absolute: raw, dry, natural, commercial, traditional, modern. I am more interested in practical questions: what are we feeding, where does it come from and is it appropriate for this individual Cane Corso?

sections.heading: The old rural diet
paragraphs: Dr. Flavio Bruno describes working dogs in the traditional rural South eating foods drawn from the same agricultural economy in which they lived. Animal products, offal, scraps and bread could all be part of that context. People often knew directly where the food came from.

sections.heading: History is not automatically a prescription
paragraphs: A historical description tells us what people did; it does not automatically tell every modern owner what they should do today. Food-safety knowledge changes, veterinary nutrition develops and individual health conditions differ.

sections.heading: My own approach
paragraphs: In correspondence I described my own routine: a complete dry food as the regular base, with selected fresh animal foods whose origin I try to know and with attention to freshness, storage and hygiene. That is personal practice, not a universal instruction.

sections.heading: The puppy is not a small adult
paragraphs: A recently weaned puppy must support growth as well as maintenance. This is one reason feeding should not become an improvised experiment or a race to make a puppy grow faster.

sections.heading: Quality before ideology
paragraphs: Useful questions include whether the diet is complete, whether the source is trustworthy, whether storage and hygiene are safe and whether the individual Cane Corso has a medical condition that changes its needs.

sections.heading: The purpose of food
paragraphs: Food should support life, growth, health, movement, recovery, reproduction when relevant and ageing. The goal is not to win an argument about diet; the goal is to care properly for the Cane Corso in front of us.

title: Responsible Breeding
subtitle: A Litter Is Not the End of the Responsibility
summary: Reproduction creates long-term obligations: selection, health, family knowledge, placement and responsibility for the lives produced.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: USG breeding philosophy based on Stefano De Tanini’s stated practices and correspondence.

sections.heading: Ask why before which pair
paragraphs: Making puppies is easy. Taking responsibility for why they were born is something else. A mating should have a reason: what are we trying to preserve, what weaknesses are present and what do we actually know about the male and female?

sections.heading: Selection is responsibility
paragraphs: Dr. Flavio Bruno repeatedly brings selection back to type and function. For me, health must stand beside that principle. Character, structure and what the parents transmit all matter.

sections.heading: Family knowledge has value
paragraphs: I have tried to follow continuity in my own Cane Corso over generations. I do not present that as an official pedigree. It is a family archive of animals I have known: appearance, behaviour, offspring and traits that reappeared.

sections.heading: Avoid biological shortcuts
paragraphs: In my own approach I have deliberately avoided close inbreeding. That is a personal breeding principle grounded in my priority for health, character and respect for the animals.

sections.heading: Responsibility continues after placement
paragraphs: The puppy leaves, but the story does not end. I want to know where it goes, who will raise it and whether the person understands Cane Corso. If I believe the person is wrong for the puppy, I prefer to refuse.

sections.heading: Breeding is not production
paragraphs: A mother is not a production unit. A male is not simply a genetic tool. A puppy is not inventory. If I choose to bring a life into the world, I accept responsibility for what I am creating.

title: Research Before Legend
subtitle: How Cane Corso Heritage Should Treat History
summary: USG should distinguish documents, testimony, interpretation and hypothesis so that passion never becomes invented certainty.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: USG research method developed through correspondence and revision work with Dr. Flavio Bruno.

sections.heading: Breed history attracts legends
paragraphs: An old painting appears. A powerful dog resembles Cane Corso. Someone creates a story. The story is repeated until repetition becomes “evidence”. I do not want Cane Corso Heritage to work that way.

sections.heading: Memory is valuable
paragraphs: Personal testimony matters. The memories of veterinarians, farmers, shepherds, hunters and old families may preserve a world that would otherwise disappear. But memory and documentary proof are not identical.

sections.heading: A document must be examined
paragraphs: When Dr. Flavio Bruno shared old references, paintings, quotations and the Mario Monti material, I stated that names, titles, dates and quotations should be checked individually before definitive publication. A transcription error should not weaken a valuable argument.

sections.heading: Four levels of evidence
paragraphs: USG should distinguish documented source, personal testimony, interpretation and hypothesis. A documented source can be checked; testimony belongs to an identified person; interpretation explains; hypothesis asks a question not yet established.

sections.heading: An image is not automatically proof
paragraphs: An old strong dog in an Italian painting may be fascinating, but resemblance alone does not prove breed identity. If author, period or provenance are unknown, that uncertainty should remain visible.

sections.heading: Correcting ourselves is research
paragraphs: I have changed my own ideas many times during conversations with Dr. Bruno. That does not embarrass me. Accepting a correction is more important than defending an idea because it was mine.

sections.heading: Heritage does not need mythology
paragraphs: The real history of Cane Corso is already extraordinary. Respecting uncertainty is not weakness. Preserve the memory, check the evidence, separate fact from interpretation and keep searching.

title: Cane Corso Heritage
subtitle: What We Are Trying to Preserve
summary: The editorial manifesto for USG Cane Corso Heritage: preserve function, character, stories, responsibility, evidence and the human world around the breed.
author: Stefano De Tanini
source_credit: USG editorial manifesto by Stefano De Tanini.

sections.heading: More than beautiful images
paragraphs: Cane Corso Heritage was not born because the world needed another page of beautiful Cane Corso photographs. Beautiful images have their place, but they are not enough. I wanted a place where Cane Corso could be understood through history, function, character, human relationships, rural culture, health, responsibility, memory and real lives.

sections.heading: A living heritage
paragraphs: A breed is not simply measurements, pedigree, standard or today's image. Behind the modern Cane Corso are people, places, needs, work, families, successes, mistakes and generations of animals whose lives created the road to the present.

sections.heading: Function
paragraphs: Dr. Flavio Bruno gave me the principle that became central to the way I study Cane Corso: “La funzione fa il tipo” — Function creates type. The sentence connects body to work, character to necessity, territory to morphology and human to Cane Corso.

sections.heading: Coscienza
paragraphs: Then came another word: “coscienza”. The Cane Corso that understands its human, for which sometimes a look is enough. That idea connects function with relationship because the Cane Corso was not simply strong; it had to observe, understand and remain connected.

sections.heading: Stories
paragraphs: Heritage also lives in stories: Reia; the young Flavio beside the old veterinarian; Leone the Mastino; Spezzaferro; the porcaio and his Cane Corso; the old families and the dogs whose names survive because somebody remembered them.

sections.heading: Responsibility
paragraphs: Admiration is not enough. If we celebrate Cane Corso without teaching responsibility, we have done half the work. Power requires knowledge, consistency, care, health, education, time and a human prepared to remain responsible when life becomes difficult.

sections.heading: Science and memory
paragraphs: History deserves respect. Veterinary science deserves respect. Personal experience deserves respect. But they are not the same thing. An old feeding practice is history; a veterinary recommendation is medicine; a personal observation is experience; a hypothesis is a question; a verified document is evidence.

sections.heading: No invented history
paragraphs: If we do not know, we should say we do not know yet. If Dr. Flavio Bruno tells a personal story, we identify it as his. If I express an interpretation, it carries my name. If evidence requires verification, we say so. If better evidence proves one of my ideas wrong, the idea must change.

sections.heading: USG — Unico Suo Genere
paragraphs: For me Cane Corso has never been simply another dog. It is presence, character, intelligence, strength, dignity, function, responsibility and a bond with the human. That is why I chose Unico Suo Genere — unique in its kind — not only as a name, but as an expression of how I understand Cane Corso.

sections.heading: What we preserve
paragraphs: We preserve stories and questions. We preserve the people who remember. We preserve the function behind the form, the importance of character, the responsibility of the human and the difference between memory and proof. Wherever evidence is incomplete, we continue searching.
Heritage is not about freezing the past. It is about making sure the past is not forgotten while we decide what deserves to continue into the future.
